e.t: This word is a proper name rendered “Abiou” or “Aviou,” identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing six times in 1 Kings and once in 1 Chronicles. The name is found in six verses, including 1 Kings 14:31 and 15:1, 7, 8, and 28, and 1 Chronicles 7:8. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adverb means acting guilelessly or honestly, without deceit or hidden motives. It describes the manner in which someone speaks, acts, or approaches something: openly, sincerely, and without trying to mislead. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 7:13. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: conduct marked by honesty rather than manipulation. The surrounding verse is needed to explain precisely how this manner of acting functions in that passage.

Azarias is a personal name used to identify someone named Azarias. As a proper noun, it does not describe an action, quality, or object; it names a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, this name occurs 34 times across 32 verses, showing that it refers to several people rather than necessarily one individual throughout the corpus. Its exact reference in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This Greek LXX noun means “brier,” referring to a prickly, thorn-bearing plant. It names vegetation that can hinder, scratch, or make a path difficult, rather than describing a person or action. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing a recurring image drawn from ordinary plant life. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a brier or thorny plant.

This adjective means “sleepless,” describing someone or something that does not sleep. It presents wakefulness as the central quality rather than naming an action or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Wisdom 7:10. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact contextual emphasis cannot be stated beyond this basic meaning. Its use is therefore best understood as a direct description of continued wakefulness.

This word means “foreigner”—a person regarded as belonging to another people or land. It can function as a noun for such a person or as an adjective describing someone or something associated with outsiders. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 281 times, showing that it is a recurring way to identify people as foreign or outside a particular community. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means sand, the many small grains found along beaches, shores, deserts, or other places where loose earth gathers. It is a noun used to name this material. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 30 times, including descriptions of something numerous or spread out like sand. Its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: physical sand, while the surrounding verse determines whether it is being counted, gathered, crossed, or used as a comparison. The word appears in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical portions of this Greek corpus.

gl: proclaim by voice of herald; publish abroad
d: proclaim by voice of herald; publish abroad

e.t: This verb means to proclaim something publicly, like a herald announcing it, or to publish it abroad. It describes making a message known openly and widely rather than keeping it private. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) material represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 17:23. The word itself identifies the act of public announcement; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what was proclaimed there.

This adjective describes someone as “unindicted” or “without accusation”—a person against whom no accusation is being brought. It presents accusation as absent, rather than naming a positive quality or explaining why the person stands without accusation. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “worth”—the value, significance, or deserving quality of a person or thing. As a noun, it identifies what something is considered to be worth rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it appears seven times, including passages in Job, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its precise emphasis can depend on what person or thing is being evaluated in the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains value or worth.

This verb means “give,” describing the act of providing or handing something to another. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding words determine what is given and to whom, but its central meaning remains the transfer or granting of something. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s context.

This adjective describes something that is improper, unsuitable, or out of place—something that does not fit what is fitting or respectable. It can describe conduct, behavior, or an appearance judged inappropriate. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is clearly “unseemly” or “unbecoming.”

The word means a “joint”: a point where separate parts meet or are connected. It is a noun naming that meeting point rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Sirach and once in 4 Maccabees. Without the verse text, the exact kind of joint and its particular force in either passage cannot be stated more precisely. Its central idea remains connection at the meeting point of parts.

This word is a proper name, referring to Arsinoe, also given as Arsini. It functions as a personal name rather than a common description or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees, at 1:1 and 1:4. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the person being mentioned, while the passage supplies the details about her role or circumstances.

This Greek LXX noun means “dishonor”: a condition of shame, disgrace, or lost respect. It describes the opposite of being treated with honor and can refer to the humiliation or disgrace associated with wrongdoing, foolish conduct, or a lowered standing. The word occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented in this corpus, showing that it is used broadly for disgrace rather than for one narrowly defined event. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Achinaam is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament, rendered “Achinaam” or “Akhinaam.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Samuel and once in 1 Chronicles. The available references establish where the name occurs, but without the surrounding verse text, this name’s particular role in each passage cannot be explained here.

Baada is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action or quality. The name is also given as “Vaatha” in the lexical definition. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:8. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular family or historical setting must be understood from that passage, but its basic function is clear: it is a personal name used to identify an individual.

Banaias, also rendered Vaneas, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person by name. It occurs 28 times across 28 verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying reference to the person who bears it; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in any particular passage.

This noun means a realm or kingdom—the domain ruled by a king or governing authority. It can refer to an earthly political territory, such as a kingdom among the nations, and its broad use in the Greek Old Testament includes both historical and prophetic writings. The word occurs 340 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains a defined realm under rule.

“Bougathan” or “Vugathan” is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 7:9. The two forms are renderings of the same named individual in this lexical entry; they do not provide a broader general meaning like a common noun. Its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative.

“Gezoue” or “Yezue” is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a person rather than describing an action or quality. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX text, with both occurrences appearing in 1 Chronicles 2:46. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an English sense or a verse-level description of the person. Its precise significance therefore comes from the surrounding genealogical context.

Damasek is a proper name referring to the place known as “Damasek” or “Thamasek.” It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a place-name used to identify a specific location. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Kings 11:14. The two forms preserve the same named place while reflecting different ways of representing its name. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the events being described there.

This is a proper name for Deuteronomy, the biblical book known in Greek as “Deuteronomion” or “Thefteronomion.” The name identifies the book rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Deuteronomy 17:18 and once in Joshua 9:2. Those references confirm its use as a book title, while the lexical glosses preserve the two Greek naming forms.

e.h: A Word for Way Of Spending Time
e.t: This word is a noun that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Its basic sense is “way of spending time”. It describes the manner in which someone spends time or occupies themselves, rather than naming a specific activity. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, including passages in Leviticus, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “house,” referring to a dwelling or building. It is a noun used for a physical structure rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Ezra 6:4, and its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea is therefore straightforward: a house or constructed place. Because the available wording gives only this basic sense, broader symbolic or spiritual meanings should not be assigned to the word by itself.

This verb means “bury”: to place a dead person in a grave. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented by this LXX entry, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:9. The available lexical definition gives the word’s basic action, while the verse’s surrounding text would be needed to explain the particular circumstances or emphasis there. Thus, its ordinary sense is the act of burying.

This Greek LXX verb means to “drag” or “pull” something from one place or position to another. It describes forceful movement, whether an object or person is being drawn along. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Psalms and once in Jeremiah, showing this basic sense in more than one passage. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains moving something by pulling or dragging it.

This Greek LXX verb means “select” or “choose”: to pick one person, place, or thing from among others. It describes a deliberate act of selection rather than mere observation or discovery. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 135 times, mainly in Old Testament books, and often expresses choosing among alternatives. The same basic idea can apply to people, locations, or appointed purposes, while the surrounding verse determines what is being selected. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the context.

Emmath is a proper name used for a specific place or location, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 21:32. Because the name itself is the complete meaning supplied here, it should be understood as identifying Emmath without adding an inferred definition or symbolic sense. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but lexically it functions as a place-name.

This word means “in front” or “before.” It describes something positioned ahead of another person or thing, and it can also express being in someone’s presence or prior position. As a preposition or adverb, it relates people, objects, or actions to what is ahead or previously placed. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 137 times, showing regular use for spatial and relational positioning. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “insight”—the ability to perceive or understand something clearly. It describes inward understanding that helps a person recognize what is wise, sound, or fitting. In Proverbs, it is associated with learning, discretion, knowledge, and guarded conduct, showing that insight is meant to guide life rather than remain merely intellectual. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including twelve occurrences in Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse is shaped by the surrounding passage.

“Make equal” is the central meaning of this Greek LXX verb. It describes an action that brings things into equality or treats them as equal, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Exodus, so its use is limited in this corpus. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word means “from outside” or “outer.” It describes something located beyond an inner area, coming from outside, or relating to the exterior. As an adverb or preposition, it can indicate where something is or the direction from which it comes. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 44 times, showing regular use for physical position, movement, and distinction between what is inside and what is outside. The surrounding passage determines which aspect is emphasized in a particular verse.

ἐπαίρω means to lift up or rear up. It is a verb describing the act of raising something or someone upward, or bringing something into a lifted position. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 78 times, making it a regularly used action word rather than a rare expression. Its exact force—what is being raised and why—comes from the sentence and surrounding passage.

This adjective means “listening,” describing someone who gives attention or is ready to hear. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used twice, both times in 2 Chronicles. Its basic sense points to attentive hearing rather than merely possessing the physical ability to hear. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis is on someone being attentive, receptive, or ready to respond, but the word itself centers on listening. It appears in 2 Chronicles 6:40 and 7:15.

This noun means “conversion”: a turning or change of direction, especially the idea of turning toward a new course. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times across Judges, Ezekiel, Sirach, and Song of Songs. The word’s basic sense remains focused on a turning or change rather than describing a person, place, or action by itself. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “that which is asked” or “question.” It refers to something put forward for an answer—an inquiry or matter being asked about—rather than to the answer itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Sirach 33:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from its context, but its basic sense remains an asked matter or question.

This noun means “partner,” referring to a person connected with another in a shared relationship or association. It identifies someone in relation to another person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 25 times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used as a normal relational term in several settings. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “thrive”: to grow well, prosper, or flourish. As a verb, it describes a condition or process of doing well rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, showing that it can describe flourishing as a general condition across different passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains growth, prosperity, or healthy flourishing.

This Greek LXX verb means to commend or acclaim—to express approval and praise toward someone. It describes an act of honoring or speaking favorably, rather than merely identifying a person or thing. The word appears 356 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is a broadly used verb in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX word means “have” or “hold.” As a verb, it describes possessing, keeping, or having something in one’s control, with the surrounding sentence showing the precise sense. It occurs 412 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented in this corpus, so it is a broad and ordinary word rather than a specialized term. Its meaning may concern ownership, possession, or simply having something present, depending on the context.

This Greek LXX verb means “paint from life; paint.” It describes the act of producing a painted image or representation, with the wording able to emphasize painting from a living subject. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, in passages from Isaiah, Ezekiel, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being painted and how the surrounding sentence uses the verb.

This word means “mortar,” the bowl-shaped tool used for crushing or grinding food and other substances. It is a noun naming an object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 11:8. The precise significance of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the grinding vessel itself.

This LXX word denotes “10” and is identified with “yodh.” As an indeclinable number, it functions as a fixed numerical designation rather than as a descriptive action word or title. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Psalm 118:73. The available information establishes its lexical value, but not the wording or immediate point of that verse itself.

Ibanaa; Ivanaa is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:8. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name alone does not identify the person’s role, family connection, or significance in that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a proper name: it distinguishes one person in the genealogical or community record.

This verb means to rob temples—that is, to steal from a place dedicated to worship. It describes the act of plundering sacred property rather than simply taking something from an ordinary location. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:2. The reference identifies its only occurrence, while the word’s central meaning remains the deliberate theft of temple goods or possessions. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Imarē, also rendered Imari, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:36, identifying an individual in a genealogy. Because the available information preserves the name but does not provide an additional definition or contextual description, its ordinary significance is simply the identification of that person. The name’s precise historical or family significance must be understood from the surrounding genealogical passage.

This adjective describes someone whose voice is “checked” or who is “stuttering.” It refers to difficulty expressing speech smoothly or clearly, rather than identifying the content of what is said. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus, so its established use is narrow and specific. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how this description functions in each occurrence. [p03:word:lxx:L706854:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L706854:occurrences]

Kain, also rendered Ken, is a proper name for a person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 17 times, beginning in Genesis 4:1 and appearing chiefly in Genesis, with one later occurrence in 4 Maccabees. Because it is a personal name rather than a general descriptive word, its basic meaning is identification: it names Kain in the passages where the name appears. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what is being said about him in any particular occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means a “covering” or “curtain”—something used to cover an object or form a hanging barrier. It appears 11 times in the Old Testament Greek corpus, with occurrences in Exodus, Numbers, and Isaiah. The word therefore refers to a physical covering rather than an action or abstract idea. Its exact function in any particular passage depends on what the surrounding text says is being covered or separated.

This adjective describes someone or something as “accursed” or “abominable.” It marks the person or thing as under a curse or as morally repulsive and unacceptable, rather than merely unpleasant. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice: once in 2 Maccabees 12:35 and once in 4 Maccabees 4:5. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what it describes in either passage.

This verb means to “draw up in order; arrange.” It describes putting people or things into an ordered arrangement rather than leaving them scattered or unorganized. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within four verses—three in Job and one in Ezekiel. The basic idea remains the deliberate ordering or assigning of something. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is being arranged.

This verb means “talk emptily”: to speak without useful or meaningful content. It describes empty speech rather than a substantial message. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX entry, the word occurs once, at Isaiah 8:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains speech that lacks substance or value.

This noun refers to hollowness or something hollow—an empty space or interior lacking fullness. It presents the idea of emptiness in a straightforward way, rather than naming a person, action, or emotion. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:18. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context, but its central meaning remains the condition or quality of being hollow.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “bosom” or a “bay.” As “bosom,” it names the area of the chest or the fold where something or someone may be held. As “bay,” it refers to a curved inlet of water. The word occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, so its exact sense depends on whether the passage speaks of a person’s body or a geographical feature.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “lawsuit.” It refers to a legal case or dispute brought for judgment, rather than to an ordinary disagreement. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in four different verses. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being discussed, but its central idea remains a lawsuit or formal legal proceeding.

This word means “bowl,” referring to a physical vessel or container. It is a noun, so it names the object itself rather than an action, quality, or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times in four verses spanning Exodus, 1 Kings, and Zechariah. The word keeps this straightforward object sense across its recorded uses; the surrounding passage determines the bowl’s particular purpose or setting in each verse.

This Greek LXX noun refers to speaking or saying—the act or content of expressing words. It can describe speech as something spoken, rather than naming a person or action by itself. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including uses in Esther, Job, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains speech or spoken expression.

This word is a proper name, given in the forms “Magdōlou” and “Magtholu.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs four times, in Exodus, Numbers, and Ezekiel. Its precise referent and significance in any particular verse must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text, which is not included here.

Makenia is a proper name, functioning as the identifying name of a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. Its meaning is not given as a descriptive word or action; the supplied lexical definition is simply “Makenia.” It occurs once in the Greek text, at 1 Chronicles 15:18. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the name itself can be explained, but the specific identity it designates must be determined from that passage’s context.

“Mēdikē” or “Mithiki” is a proper name identifying a particular named subject. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this name occurs once, in Daniel 9:1. The lexical meaning identifies it as a name rather than a general descriptive word, but the available information does not specify the name’s exact referent. That must be determined from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

This noun refers to dirtiness or pollution—something viewed as defiled or contaminated. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Jeremiah and 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning concerns uncleanness rather than a person, action, or object specified by itself; the surrounding verse identifies what is polluted or defiled. The word is rendered “pollution” in one recorded English translation, matching its central sense.

Naboth is a proper name, also rendered as Navoth. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Numbers 32:42. The available meaning is therefore the personal designation “Nabōth” or “Navoth,” with the person’s specific significance depending on the surrounding passage rather than on a general vocabulary meaning.

This adjective means “of sickness,” describing something associated with illness or disease. It identifies a sickly or disease-related condition rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and how the described condition is being presented there. The central idea remains consistent: the word marks something as belonging to, arising from, or characterized by sickness.

This verb means to “pour out wine for drinking.” It describes the action of serving wine into drinking vessels, rather than merely referring to wine itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 5:2, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as an action word: someone pours wine so that others may drink it.

gl: crouch down on one's hams; squat
d: crouch down on one's hams; squat

e.t: ὀκλάζω is a verb meaning “crouch down on one’s hams” or “squat.” It describes lowering the body into a bent, seated-like position rather than standing upright. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs three times, so its basic physical sense is clear. The word describes a posture or movement; by itself, it does not explain why someone crouches or what that posture may signify in a particular passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “completely” or “perfectly.” It describes an action, condition, or result as whole and without deficiency, rather than partial or incomplete. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezekiel 22:30, so its precise force there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense emphasizes completeness or perfection in the way something is done or exists.

This word means “when”. It is an adverb that points to the time or circumstance in which something happens. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its role is to connect an action, statement, or event with a particular time, helping the reader understand when something takes place. The surrounding verse determines the specific event or situation being timed.

Ougaua, also written Ugava, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, quality, or idea, so its meaning is primarily its identifying use as a name rather than a concept to define. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 37:13. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

Οχοζια is a personal name, rendered as “Ochozia” or “Okhozia.” It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing in 2 Kings and 1–2 Chronicles. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily the person it designates in each passage; the surrounding verse is needed to identify which reference to that person is intended.

This word means “panther,” referring to a powerful wild animal. It is a noun used for the animal itself, not for a person, action, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hosea. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the name of this predatory animal.

“Linger” describes staying on or remaining rather than leaving promptly. It is a verb used when someone continues in a place or situation for a time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages from Genesis, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on continued presence, while the surrounding verse determines why the person stays or what makes the delay significant.

This LXX verb means “obey”: to respond to a command or authority by doing what is required. It describes willing compliance rather than merely hearing words. The word appears twice in the LXX corpus, once in Daniel and once in Sirach, so its central meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. In ordinary sentences, it functions as an action word describing a person’s response to instruction or authority.

This noun means “station for,” referring to a designated place or position intended for a particular purpose. Its wording points to a station or stopping place rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees, at 1 Maccabees 11:4 and 11:61. The precise thing or activity associated with the station must be understood from the surrounding verse, since the word itself expresses the place’s function rather than spelling out every detail.

This adverb means “mostly” or “most often,” indicating what happens in the greater part of cases or with greater frequency. It qualifies an action or statement by showing that it is generally true, rather than necessarily true every time. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 7:22. Its exact force in that verse is best understood alongside the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “borne as by wind,” describing something carried or driven along as wind carries it. It presents movement under the force of wind rather than movement by one’s own strength or direction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 2:24. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the full context. Its central idea remains being carried along by wind.

This LXX Greek verb means “act” or “enact”: to do something or carry it out. It describes purposeful action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including Proverbs, Job, Genesis, and other writings. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what action the surrounding context identifies.

This verb means “raise higher,” describing the act of lifting something or someone to a greater height or position. It expresses upward movement or elevation rather than simply carrying or moving something. In this LXX corpus, the word appears once, in 1 Maccabees 12:36. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central meaning remains the action of raising something higher.

This word describes someone who is bankrupt, beggarly, or lacking the resources needed for life. As a noun, it can refer to a poor or needy person; as an adjective, it describes a condition of severe poverty. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 114 times, showing a broad and recurring use for poverty and need. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “roam” or “rove”—to move about rather than remain in one place. It describes an action, not a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Isaiah 23:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not part of this word-level entry, the word’s precise force there must be understood from that passage’s context. Its basic sense remains movement from place to place.

This noun means “pine resin,” a sticky substance obtained from pine trees. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, all in six Old Testament verses. It is named among valuable goods or natural products, including passages in Genesis, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. The word describes a tangible material rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Salathiel, also rendered Salathil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and is used consistently as a proper name. The name occurs 12 times in 12 verses, appearing in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

This Greek LXX verb means “obscure; darken.” It describes making something dark, dim, or difficult to see or understand. This adjective means “of myrrh” or “made of myrrh.” It describes something whose material or character is connected with myrrh, a fragrant substance used in biblical settings. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself identifies myrrh as the relevant substance rather than naming a person, action, or abstract quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “soldier,” referring to a person serving in a military force. This Greek Old Testament noun means “covering” or “protection.” It refers to something that covers or shields, whether understood physically or in a related protective sense. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Deuteronomy: Deuteronomy 23:1 and Deuteronomy 27:20. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a covering that provides protection.

Commixture refers to things joined together as a mixture or combined mass. It is a noun, naming the resulting combination rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, with one occurrence in 2 Kings 14:14 and one in 2 Chronicles 25:24. Its basic sense remains focused on mixture or commingling; the surrounding verse determines precisely what has been combined.

This adjective describes something covered by dense shade, or lying in a place where the shade is close and heavy. It presents shade as concentrated rather than thin or scattered. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Kings, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic idea remains something strongly enclosed or darkened by shade.

This adjective describes something enclosed by walls or a place under siege—“enclosed by walls; beleaguered.” It can portray fortified cities and places surrounded or defended by walls. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, chiefly in descriptions of cities and fortified locations. Its precise emphasis—physical fortification or the pressure of being besieged—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This verb means to tax by assessment: to determine an amount owed and impose that charge. It describes a governmental or administrative action rather than a general word for giving, paying, or collecting money. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 23:35. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how the action functions there, but the word itself centers on assigning a tax according to an assessment.

This Greek LXX noun means “vintage,” referring to the season or produce of gathering grapes. It describes the grape harvest as a recognizable agricultural time or yield. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages from Leviticus, Judges, Samuel, Isaiah, Amos, Joel, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the vintage—the grape harvest or its produce.

This verb means to “rule as a tyrant” or “tyrannize”—to exercise power in a harsh, oppressive, or domineering way. It describes what a ruler or authority does when control is imposed without gentleness or justice. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs four times, including once in Proverbs, twice in Wisdom, and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

“Fight for” is a verb describing active struggle on behalf of someone or something.
